title_original: Paul Nicklen, With All Due Reverence
excerpt_original: “It’s pouring rain, so it’s beautiful. The land needed it.” Paul Nicklen picks up the phone in Kenya, slightly out of breath, after it buzzed for a long time at the bottom of a pocket. He and his wife, the photographer Cristina Mittermeier, have just moved onto the lands of…

blocks.text: “It’s pouring rain, so it’s beautiful. The land needed it.” Paul Nicklen picks up the phone in Kenya, slightly out of breath, after it buzzed for a long time at the bottom of a pocket. He and his wife, the photographer Cristina Mittermeier, have just moved onto the lands of Segera, in the heart of Laikipia, and the house is still full of boxes. The week before, he flew his new plane, a Super Cub, a small high-winged bush plane, all the way from South Africa himself. A strange destination for a man of the poles, who long kept the continent at arm’s length, out of clear-sightedness. “It’s so beautiful, and it’s been photographed so heavily by my peers at National Geographic , and so many good photographers, like Nick Brandt, have worked here,” he explains. “I knew the second I came to Africa that I would fall in love with it and it would be hard to keep me away.” A correct prediction. A first flight over the savanna, love at first sight, a plane ordered on the spot. It looks a lot like the way he works: long patience, then momentum.

blocks.alt: Leopard resting on a branch, Segera, Laikipia, Kenya
blocks.caption: Leopard, Segera, Laikipia, Kenya © Paul Nicklen

blocks.text: Reverence begins with a trail. The one Louise Jeannine Roy, Paul Nicklen’s mother, climbed every morning for 15 years on Vancouver Island, up to a clearing overlooking the Strait of Georgia. A septuagenarian in top shape, a realtor, a dancer in her kitchen to the sound of Leonard Cohen, she died of a brain tumor. A few weeks later, behind the wheel, her son still asked Siri to call Mom. Then he made the climb alone, with the two dogs rescued from the beaches of Baja California, and performed his mother’s ritual: turning toward the four directions. To the east, his parents and the Saskatchewan farm, where every summer a calf became his friend before disappearing. To the north, Kimmirut, on Baffin Island, an Inuit village of 190 people, with no telephone, no television, no radio, where the boy whistled at the northern lights to make them come closer. To the south, 20 years of assignments for National Geographic . To the west, British Columbia and SeaLegacy, the organization he founded with Cristina. A table of contents, in short, drawn by a compass.

Hence the first chapter, “Matriarchs.” “I’ve spent my lifetime around wildlife and animals,” says Paul Nicklen. “It’s one thing to be a big male out there just surviving and breeding and eating. And then I just think of the hardships mothers go through.” He mentions polar bears, the females fasting all summer on land like the males, then shutting themselves in their dens for another four months without food, long enough to give birth and nurse. “I’m just in awe of females.” The image that truly opens the book shows what he means: in Tonga, a humpback whale cradles her calf under her chin above a white sandy bottom, a ring of remoras around her belly like a hula dancer’s grass skirt. That day, the photographer stayed for three hours, making some 40 breath-hold dives of 90 seconds each, until the mother slid the tip of her pectoral fin, more than 15 feet long, between them. A boundary drawn, a boundary respected. “No photograph is ever worth stressing out or upsetting an animal,” he says. When he climbed back onto the boat at sunset, the whale and her calf had not moved an inch.

blocks.text: Curiously, the foreword is signed by Mother Earth. The device could seem naive, but it turns out to be delightfully frank, since the planet catches her portraitist red-handed in his clumsiness: “I have watched him fumble on the ice, misjudge the light, and surface from my waters with empty frames.” Paul Nicklen owns it. “I probably fail 98% of the time, and that’s just part of the journey. I think it’s beautiful in a way.” He recalls an encounter in the Azores with a 90-foot female blue whale, capable of engulfing the volume of an Olympic swimming pool in a single mouthful, of which no image found its way into the book.

It all began with a blur. At 15, on a family trip to Italy, his mother, a schoolteacher and amateur photographer who had set up a darkroom at home, lent him her Pentax K1000. At 18, as a biology student at the University of Victoria, Paul Nicklen still struggled to get his pictures in focus. Bad grades too, for lack of concentration in class: he only discovered much later that he has attention deficit disorder. A late focus. A curious paradox for a man capable of waiting five years for narwhals, and who only sits still on the ice or underwater. His eye was born after his studies, in the Barren Lands, the vast tundra between Nunavut and the Northwest Territories, where a pilot dropped him off alone for three months. More than 600 miles on foot and by canoe, 50 pounds lost, wolves, musk oxen, a golden eagles’ nest. “I felt like a wild animal myself,” he sums up. Then came his mentors, Flip Nicklin and Joel Sartore, and National Geographic .

His signature comes down to one word: proximity. Paul Nicklen works up close, often with a wide-angle lens, the animal filling the frame. His emperor penguins bursting out of the water were shot at 16-35mm, at 1/1250th of a second. The dome port of his underwater housing bears the marks of his subjects: a sperm whale calf gummed it like a puppy, a female leopard seal confronted her own reflection in it, jaws wide open. Hence his fondness for a very different temperament, that of Vincent Munier, with his mists and distant silhouettes captured with a telephoto lens. He showed Munier’s work in his SoHo gallery in New York, hailing “the extremely talented Vincent Munier,” while knowing that this way of seeing belongs to the Frenchman from the Vosges. His own art rests on a kind of humility before error. “I’ve made so many mistakes around them, and they’re so forgiving,” he recently told his alma mater. “They look at your stupidity, and they just sort of casually walk around you.” His images? “I’m proud of my pictures, but I don’t ever look at my pictures and go, wow, those are good. I think nature is perfect.” Only one hangs in his home: the polar bear at the cabin window.

blocks.text: He edited the book alone, facing his archive: 2.5 million photographs taken over 30 years. “With National Geographic , you thought about the story first, and then often with a lot of books, you think about the geography, whether it’s the Arctic or Antarctic or the Serengeti Plains. And for me, I didn’t care.” Emotion alone counts, hence chapters titled like poems, “Ancient Wisdom,” “Emerald Seas,” “Other Nations,” and a free flow from one continent to another. The captions are moved to the back of the book, letting the spreads breathe in the large format (12.5 by 15 inches, 360 pages, printed in Paris by Printmodel). What follows reads like a family album: a coastal wolf pup, proud as a page boy, carrying an eagle feather almost as long as itself (British Columbia); a lion cub staring at its reflection in the lens (Namiri Plains, Tanzania); Craig, the last of the great elephants whose tusks reached the ground, who died of old age at 54 (Amboseli, Kenya); a polar bear poking her head through a cabin window in the middle of a blizzard, lit by the screen of a laptop the photographer holds in his left hand (Svalbard). A stroke of genius.

blocks.text: There is also Ma’ah, “grandmother” in Sm’algyax, the language of the Gitga’at. Paul Nicklen searched for this Kermode bear, a variety of black bear with white fur, sacred to the First Nations, as early as 1997, without success. Another failure in 2009. In 2010, a few days were enough, thanks to the Gitga’at and the guide Marven Robinson: Ma’ah appeared among the red clusters of a crabapple tree, the image made the cover of National Geographic , and the Northern Gateway pipeline project, which would have brought oil tankers into these fjords, was eventually abandoned thanks to activists, scientists and Indigenous communities. Nine years later, he found her again, the fur thinning around her eyes. “It’s the first time I’ve really had a chance to publish my spirit bear pictures inside a book,” he says. Ma’ah, for her part, still has no idea of the role she played.

blocks.alt: White spirit bear standing among crabapple branches with red fruit, British Columbia
blocks.caption: Ma’ah, the spirit bear, among crabapples, Great Bear Rainforest, British Columbia © Paul Nicklen

blocks.alt: White spirit bear walking on mossy rocks, British Columbia
blocks.caption: Ma’ah, nine years later, British Columbia © Paul Nicklen

blocks.alt: Spirit bear sitting between giant trees in a mossy rainforest
blocks.caption: Spirit bear in the Great Bear Rainforest, British Columbia © Paul Nicklen

blocks.text: He is sometimes called “too National Geographic ,” a prisoner of the spectacular. The facts tell another story. With more than 7 million followers on Instagram, Paul Nicklen is the most followed wildlife photographer on the platform, and one of the most followed photographers in the world, all genres combined. In Hartley Bay, the Gitga’at elder Helen Clifton held up the magazine with Ma’ah on the cover and told him: “We did this together.” Among the Inuit, he learned to listen more, talk less and never brag. The acknowledgments in Reverence run for pages, naming his Inuit companions from Canada and Greenland, the Maasai guides who led him to Craig, pilots, captains, and three late friends whose laughter he will never forget. He locates his loneliness elsewhere: in hotel rooms in big cities, after giving talks. “When I’m in nature, I’m never lonely.” As for National Geographic , he owes it everything, and left it for precisely that reason: “It’s great to have 100 million people plus see your story on National Geographic , but if you’re not affecting change, then what’s the point?” Hence SeaLegacy, the SoHo gallery, the fine art prints, and this book whose cover, a whale and her calf in black and white, has more of the print than of the documentary plate.

Another long wait. For 30 years, Paul Nicklen dreamed of getting close to a puma. On Vancouver Island, home to the densest cougar population in the world, he had only glimpsed one, scurrying back into the brush. In Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, his guide Rodrigo Moraga led him to a young female he had known since she was born. A snowstorm rose, and they sheltered in the same cave. “She never looked at me once. She was just looking across the valley waiting for guanacos to come out during a storm so she could go hunting,” he remembers. As she left, she brushed against his leg, “basically zero centimeters away.” Tears. Rodrigo smiled and simply said: “I know.” The emotion, the photographer explains, lies above all in the place: an estancia that decided these cats, long shot by ranchers, were worth more alive. “Now to see 10 a day, it’s really special.” In the book, we meet Petaka, another female, lying beneath a rainbow or looking up at an Andean condor with the nonchalance of a queen.

blocks.text: The poles remain his kingdom. His emperor penguins bursting from the water in a trail of microbubbles, an image that won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition in 2011, came from a tip by his Swedish friend Göran Ehlmé, who had filmed the phenomenon ten years earlier for the BBC. Nicklen barely believed it. Two and a half months alone on the Antarctic sea ice, diving whenever possible, until the day the birds released the air from their feathers and rocketed to the surface. Older still, the narwhal saga lasted five years: a parasail towed by a snowmobile, a fall into a meltwater pool, an ultralight flown with his high school friend Brian Knutsen, and finally, landed on a single ice floe, a thousand tusks breaking the surface. Right after, the rotten ice gave way beneath his feet and his shoulder was dislocated; it took nearly an hour to put it back in place. He smiled the whole time. The shoulder was replaced last summer.

blocks.text: These images fund everything else. “Everything I do is sort of the intersection of art, science and conservation,” sums up Paul Nicklen, who makes his living selling his prints. It has to be beautiful, grounded in fact, and moving. Such as his ice waterfall, meltwater pouring off the Nordaustlandet ice cap in Svalbard, which Pearl Jam chose for the cover of their 2020 album Gigaton . Or his aerial views, almost watercolors: tannin-stained rivers winding between the white dunes of Lençóis Maranhenses in Brazil, the branching channels of the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, where the river no longer reaches the sea.

blocks.text: Seen from above, everything is reframed. And with all due reverence, Paul Nicklen dares to say what many believers will find provocative. “People live their lives on this planet as if they’re gonna go see some dude in a white robe waiting for them, and they often are disrespectful of this planet. For me, I’ve always said heaven is here and now.” He remembers a dinner with Elon Musk and his horror at the Martian dream: “That’s hell. Like, to live with a bunch of humans under a glass dome, with air that you can’t breathe, there’s no water to drink. Where is the romance in that when you think of 4 billion years arriving at this point with this incredibly precious planet?”

And artificial intelligence, capable of generating a pod of narwhals in seconds? “I can spot AI pretty easily, and I’m not too worried about it,” he replies. His sadness goes to young photographers starting out in this new world. “It’s more, what is the story worth? What is honest journalism? Using powerful photography to bring people into the conversation.” Why, then, wonder rather than alarm, when the book points out that wildlife populations have fallen by nearly 70% in 50 years? “Hope is the only emotion really greater than fear.” What he hopes for from the reader follows from this, and fits in a few words: close the book, go outside, look around, and let that beauty weigh on everyday choices. He has not forgotten the starving polar bear filmed in 2017 and seen by a quarter of the planet, and he argues for mixing registers. Still, Reverence leans firmly toward wonder, down to the tiny creatures of the Lembeh Strait in Indonesia, explored at night on a rebreather: an emperor shrimp riding a nudibranch, an octopus hauling two halves of a shell like a caravan and shutting itself in at the slightest doubt. Breathtaking.

blocks.text: This wonder comes from far away, from the boy of Kimmirut and his long nights without television, when stories were told in stone. “I saw beluga whales in carvings before I saw them in the wild,” says Paul Nicklen, who keeps at home a soapstone carving of two brothers fighting over the first seal, the elder having stolen the younger one’s catch. “Such powerful, evocative, visceral storytelling,” he says, which taught him to see the world in shapes, colors and stories. As for Cristina, his diving and fieldwork partner, she sees differently: “She’s all about the empty spaces and I’m all about getting that animal to be in my face and be close.” A two-voice book is in the works, possibly called “Side by Side.” They are approaching 60, he reckons they have “15, 16 years left,” and they fully intend to enjoy them.

blocks.alt: Close-up of an orca's white eye patch underwater in deep blue
blocks.caption: Orca, underwater © Paul Nicklen

blocks.text: Reverence by Paul Nicklen is published by Hemeria (360 pages, from $124) in English and French editions. The photographer will sign copies at Paris Photo on Friday November 13, 2026, at 3 p.m., at the Hemeria booth (P19, Galerie Courbe Sud), Grand Palais, Paris.
